noveltyJustification: Allowlist lever, cascade math, dispute analogue, and failure-semantics finding are new; cost anatomy refines iteration 1.
keyQuestions: How can grader accuracy be raised or cost lowered?
answeredQuestions: How can grader accuracy be raised or cost lowered?

text: Cost is linear in reruns x rows: planned 3K+1 calls (169 for K=56), reruns are 168/169 calls; 33% saving if reruns drop to 2, at the price of F.
yesVotes>=2 maps ties to 'no', the majority class; corpus has zero ties and one 2-1 flip; a 4th tie/borderline call is a bounded lever.
Miss 0.43/0.43/0.40 vs worst no row 0.40/0.38/0.43; threshold 0.42 fixes the corpus miss with no no-row flip, but margin is one row and 0.03 noul: held-out hypothesis only.
0/21 fixtures carry allowlists; populating them repairs check specificity (fp mass = task names + builtins), anchors the Claude grader rubric, and lets buildState pass ground truth to the jev grader.
Cascade (check-flagged rows only) routes 43/56 today for 130 vs 169 calls (23% saving) because check fn=0; saving grows once allowlists cut the 34 false positives (unmeasured).
dispute.cjs already escalates low-confidence D4 calls (confidence<0.7 or dispute rate>0.15) to an adversarial second call; the jev arm has no analogue; 8/168 calls sit in [0.40,0.60).
In the --grader llm path a dispatch or parse failure yields score 0.0 / parse_status failed, i.e. a failed measurement reads as maximal hallucination (D4 weight 0.15).

Label/class/headroom gates already prevent spending where no verdict is decidable (470>504 passed here); answer caching is the remaining lever and trades against flip measurement, so opt-in for regression only.
Multi-row batching and cheaper JEV_PROVIDER are plausible cost levers but unmeasured; both would need a new agreement run (named UNKNOWN).
